summary:
Astro Vitals is a daily health self-check for astronauts on long missions. On the way to Mars, a crew is alone for months and a message to Earth can take more than 20 minutes. The crew must find a health problem early, and without help from the ground.

Each day, the astronaut records sleep, mood, stress, fatigue, fluid intake and exercise on a tablet, marks symptoms on a body figure, and can do a 3-minute reaction-time test. Once a week, there is a vision test. No medical device is necessary.

The tool compares each astronaut with their own baseline from 14 pre-flight days. Thirty-one rules, each with its source (NASA standards, published studies), give one of four levels: OK, self-care, tell the Crew Medical Officer, or contact the flight surgeon. An export of less than 16 KB goes to Earth.

The same engine, written in Rust, runs on desktop, in the browser and on Android, with no network. This is a prototype: all data is simulated.
details:
What it does: Astro Vitals is a daily health self-check for the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". Each day, the astronaut answers a short check-in (sleep, mood, stress, fatigue, fluid intake, exercise), marks symptoms on a body figure and can do a 3-minute psychomotor vigilance test (reaction time). A weekly vision test looks for signs of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).

How it works: During 14 pre-flight days, the tool records a personal baseline for each astronaut. In flight, a rule engine compares each value with that baseline and with thresholds from NASA sources. There are 31 rules in one TOML file. Each rule has an action, an explanation and a source URL. The result is one of four levels: OK, self-care, tell the Crew Medical Officer, or send a packet to the flight surgeon. The export packet is less than 16 KB, for a slow and delayed link to Earth.

Benefits and impact: The crew can find a problem early, without waiting for the ground. The astronaut always sees why a rule fired and where the threshold comes from. Everything works offline.

Tools: Rust (one shared rule engine, with tests), Tauri 2 and Svelte (desktop app), WebAssembly (browser demo on GitHub Pages), Expo / React Native (Android app), GitHub Actions (builds and releases).

Creativity: The same engine runs on three platforms with no network, and each astronaut is compared with their own baseline, not with a population average.

Limits: This is a prototype and not a medical device. All data is simulated. Some thresholds are design selections; the repository lists which ones.
